source.title: Protein Autoregressive Modeling via Multiscale Structure Generation
source.authors: Yanru Qu; Cheng-Yen Hsieh; Zaixiang Zheng; Ge Liu; Quanquan Gu

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports scaling experiments for protein structure generation, not language-model held-out cross-entropy or power-law fits. It cites Kaplan et al. for language-model scalability but does not test or rely on the claim in the question.
record.gate_note: The paper varies protein-model size and training duration and reports generation metrics. These results do not test the claim's language-model loss laws or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. The related protein-scaling results are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The paper is a protein backbone generation method. Its scaling sweep (decoder 60M/200M/400M by 200–600K steps, Fig. 5) reports generation-quality metrics (FPSD, fS, designability, sc-RMSD). It does not report held-out loss, does not fit a power law, and does not examine compute-optimal allocation. Kaplan et al. is cited only as evidence that AR models scale. The sweep is the authors' own method's behaviour, not a test of the power-law form in another modality. It therefore does not test V5 or any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors say PAR shows favorable scaling with decoder size and training steps on FPSD and fS. Model size, not training duration alone, drives designability and sc-RMSD gains. A small 60M AR transformer suffices, and enlarging it does not help.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not reproduce or apply the language-model loss-scaling method.
record.method_sensitivity: Protein-generation metrics vary with decoder size and training duration; the text says decoder size has stronger effects than duration alone.

fits_no_version.finding: In PAR protein backbone generation, a larger flow decoder (60M to 400M) improves designability and sc-RMSD, and FPSD/fS improve with size and steps. Extending training steps alone gives negligible gains in designability. Enlarging the AR transformer from 60M to 400M gives no improvement (Tab. 13).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Protein structure generators show monotone, non-power-law-characterised gains from decoder size, with little gain from training duration alone; this is an architecture-component-dependent effect.

record.problems: The scaling results concern protein-generation metrics rather than held-out language-model cross-entropy. The paper does not report power-law fits or individual numerical values for the plotted scaling sweeps in the text.

untested.parts: No shape sweep at fixed parameter count. The AR-vs-decoder size ablation (Tab. 13) is not a test of shape.
Protein generation metrics improve with scale, but no power-law form is fitted or tested.

record.verdict_notes: The rows are correctly unlinked. The AR-size ablation (Tab. 13: 400M AR gives 87.8% designability vs 96.0% for 60M AR with a 400M decoder) is not in the rows but bears on no version.

versions.untested_parts: The paper studies protein generation scaling, but does not test whether the same power-law form holds.
